comments.author: @jlf2221
comments.text:
It’s seems as our human reviewers system itself may be obsolete now or very soon. How can human reviewers, with much less ‘knowledge’, and less perfect ‘recall’ adequately judge the scientific merit of a submitted paper. An AI Agents reviewer group would probably give a less biased, more knowledgeable scoring to submitted papers. Possibly add several AI reviewer agents, each based on a different model, thus with different biases.
Grok says: “A panel of AI agent reviewers, each built on a different model with distinct biases, could indeed smooth out some of the quirks and blind spots that any single AI might have—sort of like how a diverse human panel balances perspectives. It’s a clever twist on ensemble methods, where multiple systems collaborate to get closer to the truth.
Here’s how it could work: Imagine three AI reviewers—one based on a model trained heavily on theoretical physics, another on experimental data, and a third on statistical rigor. The first might overvalue elegant equations, the second might obsess over lab reproducibility, and the third might nitpick p-values. When they evaluate a paper, their biases clash. The theoretical AI might love a bold new model, but the experimental one flags missing data, and the stats AI calls out shaky correlations. Together, they force a more rounded critique, catching flaws no single perspective would. It’s like a debate club—disagreement sharpens the outcome.
This setup could dampen individual biases by design. If each AI’s training data or objective function skews differently (e.g., one prioritizes novelty, another consistency with prior work), their collective judgment could approximate a more neutral stance. Studies on ensemble AI systems—like those used in machine learning competitions—show they often outperform solo models by averaging out errors. Applied to peer review, this could mean fewer papers slip through with overhyped claims or sloppy methods.”

Thanks for this illuminiating video. To me, the merit of any scientific paper is their contribution to the body of scientific knowledge. Hence, the papers submitted by the AI Scientist should be assessed based this first. comments.author: @SimonChemist
comments.text: As a biochemist, I don't fully understand how AI can create scientific results for me. AI is certainly useful for writing articles in chemistry, biology, physics, but the essence of articles in these disciplines is conducting real experiments with matter (whether living or non-living) rather than in silico. Conducting experiments to test a proposed hypothesis is a fundamental characteristic of scientific work. Writing an abstract, literature review, describing methods - these are just the shell of a scientific paper to introduce the reader to the problem being solved, but not the research itself. Mainly, scientists from natural sciences describe in articles the results of one or several successful experiments, the essence of which can be explained to a specialist in a few sentences and they will understand. LLMs can perfectly mimic scientific work, but they simply cannot take experimental data because they cannot conduct experiments. Perhaps in mathematics and computer science this approach is different, but I am not a specialist in these disciplines.

comments.author: @autarh314
comments.text:
On the topic of AI generated art (music, literature, photos) vs genuine, think of music recorded on CDs vs vinyl. A lot of audiophiles still think vinyl music sounds "better" (what they mean by "better" is not an universal measure) than digitally recorded music. The reason is precisely the imperfections that a vinyl recording brings with it - those recording "defects" are so close to being imperceptible that they turned into a feature, not a bug, whereas CD music is just "too perfect".

I think it's the same with human art vs AI generated art - as AI tools get better and better, they'll stop hallucinating, messing up hands etc, and their results will inch closer and closer to perfection, but that's precisely what will make them differ from human art. Whereas an AI generated novel will have perfect structure, grammar, flow etc (having been trained on millions of novels), humans will still make those "mistakes" (which differ greatly from one person to the next) that are linked to each individual's persona.

Regarding the question of meaning. i don't think words written by an AI have any more or less meaning. In my view, what becomes meaningless is the process of writing. If a human goes through the experience, they derive meaning from that. If I understand anything about the author, new levels of meaning become available to me as well. 

In a commercial world, everything is a product, including art. The process is supposed to be largely irrelevant.  In human life, the process and what we learn from it is all. Products are ephemeral, truth and beauty endure, and those are human experiences, not products. So I think we are moving to an age where we begin to pay attention to who is doing what, why, and what they gain from the experience. This is what we will come to value.

comments.author: @AlexAndersAuthor
comments.text:
You mentioned that story that Sam Altman posted and that you played in your video. I was someone who commented as a professional author saying that it wasn't good. I got the impression from your comments this time that you didn't fully digest the objections to it. I thought of a great analogy to help you understand why the story wasn't good.

Do you know how AI images can look fantastic. But then you look at the details like people's tattoos and you realize that it It isn't an image of anything. Or that the person's hands aren't clasped. They're melted into each other. But if you just take a glance at them, the images look fantastic. 

That's how Sam Altman's story was. Without paying close attention to what was being said, it seems like literary genius. But then if you actually pictured all the things the AI was saying, you realize it's tedious and all of those words don't amount to anything larger. It's not something that someone would actually want to read.

I am a huge supporter of AI. When it becomes helpful as a writing tool, I plan on using it. But that story wasn't good. AI is not there yet for writing stories that are actually good.

I don't think creative works of art or fiction should have to declare if they used AI. If the work connects with people, makes them feel, what should it matter? If knowing that something was created or co-created by AI lessens your connection to it somehow, due to even an unconscious bias, you're better of not knowing and just enjoying the work as you find it.
And I say that as someone who has spent decades working on his craft and being professionally published in multiple languages. It's the effect on the reader/viewer that counts, not the tools used. I do understand the bias, but I think a lot of the talk around that comes from creators who are fearful and angry, and that's not a place from which to look at things rationally.
As a consumer of fiction and art, in the sense that I want to have an experience with that work, I don't need to know if AI was involved, I just have to feel what I feel when I engage with it.
